column1: In Ia q.2, a.1, what distinction does Aquinas draw between a proposition being self-evident in itself and self-evident to us, and why does it matter?
column2: Self-evident in itself vs. to us (Ia q.2, a.1): "God exists" is self-evident in itself because God's essence is his existence — to grasp what God is would be to see that he exists. It is not self-evident to us because we do not know God's essence; we know him only through creatures. So his existence must be demonstrated from effects.

column1: Why does Aquinas say God's existence can be demonstrated only from his effects, not from his essence?
column2: Demonstration from effects (a.2): Demonstration from God's essence (propter quid) is unavailable in this life, since we do not comprehend that essence. Demonstration from effects (quia) is available: from what God causes, which is better known to us, we can prove that he exists without grasping what he is.

column1: State the difference between an essentially ordered series and an accidentally ordered (temporal) series, and explain why it matters for the First and Second Ways.
column2: Essentially vs. accidentally ordered series: An essentially ordered series is simultaneous and sustaining — each member acts only insofar as it is being acted on here and now (hand–stick–stone). An accidentally ordered series is temporal — a father begetting a son who begets a grandson, where earlier members need not still exist. The First and Second Ways concern essentially ordered series; an infinite regress there would leave the present motion or causation without a source.

column1: In the Third Way, what work does the step "if everything were contingent, at some time nothing would have existed" do, and what is the standard objection to it?
column2: The Third Way's temporal step: If everything were contingent, there would be a time when nothing existed, and from nothing nothing comes — so something necessary must exist. The standard objection is a quantifier shift: from "each contingent thing at some time does not exist" it does not follow that "at some time all contingent things simultaneously do not exist"; they could succeed one another without end.

column1: Why does the Fourth Way appeal to a maximum, and what example does Aquinas use?
column2: The Fourth Way's maximum: Things are more or less good, true, and noble, and gradations are measured against a maximum in the genus, which is the cause of the perfection in the rest — as fire, the maximum of heat, is the cause of heat in other things. So there is a maximally good, true, and noble being, the cause of those perfections in all else.

column1: What does the Fifth Way mean by "acting for an end" in things that lack intelligence, and why is the archer analogy central?
column2: Acting for an end (Fifth Way): Non-intelligent things behave regularly toward determinate outcomes, as the acorn grows toward the oak. The archer analogy matters because an arrow hits its target only as aimed: directedness without intelligence in the thing directed implies intelligence in the director.

column1: What is the force of the closing phrase of each Way, "and this everyone understands to be God"? Does it by itself establish the Christian God?
column2: And this everyone understands to be God: The phrase identifies the conclusion's referent with what "God" picks out, but does not by itself establish the Christian God in his revealed attributes. Those are argued in questions 3–11, and the Trinity and Incarnation remain, for Aquinas, matters of revelation, not demonstration.

column1: Give Aquinas's definition of law from q.90, and explain why each of its four elements is necessary.
column2: Definition of law (q.90): An ordinance of reason for the common good, made by one who has care of the community, and promulgated. Reason, because law rules and measures acts; the common good, because law aims at the community's good; the ruler, because only the one charged with the community can direct it; promulgation, because a rule cannot guide unless known.

column1: Name the four kinds of law in q.91 and state the relation between them.
column2: Four kinds of law (q.91): Eternal law (God's rational governance of the universe); natural law (rational creatures' participation in eternal law); human law (particular determinations of natural law); divine law (revealed law: Old Law and New Law). They are one order at four levels, not four competing systems.

column1: What are the two ways human law derives from natural law in q.95, a.2, and why does the distinction matter?
column2: Conclusion and determination (q.95, a.2): By conclusion, as a deduction from natural law (e.g. "do not kill" from preserving life); by determination, as a specification where natural law leaves the matter open (e.g. a particular penalty or speed limit). Conclusions bind with natural law's force; determinations bind by legitimate authority's settlement of an open question.

column1: According to q.94, a.2, what is the first principle of practical reason, and what are the three levels of inclination from which the precepts of natural law are derived?
column2: First principle and inclinations (q.94, a.2): "Good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided." The three levels of inclination: self-preservation (shared with all substances); sexual union and education of offspring (shared with animals); knowing the truth about God and living in society (proper to reason).

column1: How does q.94, a.4–a.6 qualify the universality of natural law?
column2: Qualifications (q.94, a.4–a.6): Natural law is the same for all in its first principles, but secondary conclusions vary in obviousness; it can change only by addition, not by subtraction of first principles; and while the first principles cannot be blotted out, secondary precepts can be obscured by vicious custom and corrupt habits.

column1: According to q.96, a.2–a.4, what are the limits on human law: which vices should it repress, and when does it bind in conscience?
column2: Limits on human law (q.96, a.2–a.4): Law should repress only the graver vices that harm others and threaten order, not all vices; it should prescribe only virtuous acts bearing on the common good; and it binds in conscience only insofar as it is just — an unjust law does not bind in conscience, though it may be obeyed to avoid scandal or greater disorder.

column1: Why does q.97, a.2 say human law should not be changed whenever a better law appears?
column2: Change and its cost (q.97, a.2): Change itself harms law's stability, since custom and familiarity give law its hold. A new law must therefore be sufficiently better that its benefit outweighs the damage done by changing.

column1: What is epikeia, and where does its seed appear in q.96?
column2: Epikeia (q.96, a.6): Equity — acting beside the letter of the law in a case of necessity where observing the letter would contradict the law's own purpose and the common good. The ruler's intention, not the letter alone, governs such cases.

column1: (Book I) What three conditions must the highest good satisfy, and why does wealth fail them?
column2: The highest good must be final (sought for its own sake), self-sufficient (lacking nothing when possessed), and most complete. Wealth fails because it is useful — sought for the sake of what it buys — not final.

column1: (Book I) State the function argument in three sentences, and name the step a critic is most likely to attack.
column2: The human function is activity of the soul in accordance with reason; the good of a thing is performing its function well; so the human good is such activity in accordance with virtue over a life. The most attacked step is the move from parts having functions to the whole person having one function, and from function to good — see §2(a).

column1: (Book I) Why does Aristotle say a single swallow does not make a spring — and what does the Priam example show about the limits of that point?
column2: Eudaimonia is an achievement over a complete life, not a momentary state, so one good day (a swallow) does not make a flourishing life (a spring). Priam shows the converse limit: great misfortune late in life can mar flourishing however virtuous the person, so virtue may be necessary but not sufficient for eudaimonia.

column1: (Book II) Explain the difference between virtues of thought and virtues of character, and how each is acquired.
column2: Virtues of thought are taught (through instruction and time); virtues of character are acquired by habit (by repeatedly acting as the virtuous person acts, until the disposition is settled).

column1: (Book II) Give one example of a virtue as a mean, naming both vices, and explain why the mean is not an arithmetic midpoint.
column2: Example: courage is the mean between recklessness (excess of confidence, deficiency of fear) and cowardice (deficiency of confidence, excess of fear). It is not an arithmetic midpoint because the right amount depends on the danger, the agent's capacities, and the reason for acting — the same action can be brave for one person and reckless for another.

column1: (Book III) What two conditions make an action involuntary, and why does ignorance of what one ought to know not excuse?
column2: An action is involuntary when done under compulsion (the origin is external) or through ignorance of particular circumstances, and regretted afterwards. Ignorance of what one ought to know — of general moral truths, or of facts one is responsible for knowing (as with drunkenness) — does not excuse, because the ignorance itself is blameworthy.

column1: (Book III) What is choice (prohairesis), and how does it differ from wish and from opinion?
column2: Choice is deliberate desire for what is in our power, reached through deliberation about means. It differs from wish, which can concern impossibles and ends (wishing for health, or for immortality), and from opinion, which concerns what is true or false rather than what to do.

column1: (Book IV) Why does magnanimity seem to require good fortune, and what problem does that raise for the theory?
column2: Magnanimity concerns claiming great honors one deserves, and magnificence concerns large-scale giving — both seem to require wealth and public standing. The problem: if some virtues require good fortune, then eudaimonia depends partly on luck, which sits uneasily with the idea that virtue is up to us.

column1: (Book V) Distinguish distributive from rectificatory justice, and state which proportion each uses.
column2: Distributive justice allocates divisible goods (honor, wealth) in proportion to merit, using geometric proportion. Rectificatory justice corrects wrongs by removing gain and restoring loss, treating the parties as equals, using arithmetic proportion.

column1: (Book VI) What is practical wisdom (phronēsis), and why does Aristotle say the young cannot yet have it?
column2: Practical wisdom is the virtue of deliberating well about what conduces to living well as a whole. The young cannot yet have it because it requires experience of particular situations over time — unlike mathematics, which can be grasped young.

column1: (Book VI) Why is virtue impossible without practical wisdom, and practical wisdom impossible without virtue?
column2: Virtue without practical wisdom is mere natural disposition (a child can be naturally brave without knowing why or when bravery is called for); practical wisdom without virtue is mere cleverness, which can serve bad ends. Each needs the other to be virtue in the full sense.

column1: (Book VII) How does Aristotle's account of akrasia differ from Socrates' claim that no one acts against their knowledge?
column2: Socrates claimed no one acts against their knowledge — apparent akrasia must be ignorance. Aristotle replies that the akratic person has the knowledge but fails to use it in the moment (knowing in the abstract vs. knowing actively), so he acts against a judgment he genuinely holds and regrets it afterwards.

column1: (Books VIII–IX) Name the three kinds of friendship and explain why only one is stable.
column2: Friendships of utility (based on mutual advantage), of pleasure (based on mutual enjoyment), and of the good (based on mutual recognition of character). Only the last is stable, because character is stable while utility and pleasure change; the first two dissolve when their basis ends.

column1: (Book X) Why does Aristotle argue that contemplation is more self-sufficient than ethical activity?
column2: Contemplation needs least from outside: it can be pursued alone, with fewer resources, and for longer stretches than ethical activity, which requires other people, external goods, and occasions for action. It is also loved purely for its own sake, whereas ethical actions, though choiceworthy in themselves, also serve further ends.

column1: (Whole work) State one way in which the contemplative peak of Book X creates a tension with Books I–IX, and one scholarly response to that tension.
column2: Tension: Books I–IX present flourishing as practically engaged and socially embedded, while Book X crowns a solitary, intellectual activity. Responses include: (a) contemplation is the dominant end crowning a life that still includes ethical virtue; (b) the tension reflects different strata of the treatise; (c) the two accounts describe two kinds of happiness, the divine and the human, both genuinely available. Scholars defend all three.

column1: What does Augustine mean by saying the heart is "restless until it rests in God" (I.1), and what evidence does Book I offer for the claim?
column2: The heart is made for God and finds no final rest in finite goods (I.1). Book I's evidence is developmental: even the infant's rage at a thwarted will, and the schoolboy's tears for Dido alongside indifference to his own state, show a desire that overshoots every object offered to it.

column1: Why does Augustine choose the pear theft (II.4) as his central example of evil, and what does it show that a theft for gain would not?
column2: The theft isolates the will (II.4). A theft for gain could be explained by need or profit; this theft had neither — Augustine threw the pears away — so the only explanation left is love of the transgression itself.

column1: What attracted Augustine to Manichaeism, and why did he remain only a "hearer" rather than becoming one of the elect?
column2: Manichaeism offered a rational account of evil that excused God and the agent (III.6–III.10). Augustine remained a hearer — a junior adherent — because the elect's strict ascetic discipline was a commitment he did not make.

column1: How did Cicero's Hortensius change Augustine's ambitions, and why did the Bible initially repel him?
column2: Hortensius redirected him from rhetorical success to the search for wisdom (III.4). The Bible repelled him because its style seemed crude beside Cicero and its stories, read literally, seemed unworthy of God (III.5).

column1: What does the grief for his friend in Book IV teach Augustine about loving mortal things?
column2: Love fixed on a mortal object as if it were final ends in grief (IV.4–IV.7). His home town became hateful because his friend was absent from it; the pain taught that a soul loving only what can die will itself be torn by loss.

column1: Why did Faustus' failure matter more to Augustine than a defeat in debate would have, and what did he do after leaving the Manichaeans?
column2: Faustus was the sect's great teacher, and his honest admission that he could not answer the cosmological questions showed the system itself had no answers (V.3–V.7). Augustine left the sect on intellectual grounds and suspended judgment, rather than converting immediately.

column1: How did Ambrose's allegorical preaching remove Augustine's intellectual objection to Scripture?
column2: Allegory showed the Old Testament passages that seemed crude literally could be read spiritually (V.14). The text was not the crude document he had assumed.

column1: What is the difference, in Book VI, between Augustine's intellectual convictions and his will — and what is the prayer that exposes it?
column2: By Book VI he no longer doubted that God is incorporeal or that Catholicism was more credible than Manichaeism; he was held back by habit, not argument (VI.11–VI.15). The prayer "give me chastity and continence, but not yet" exposes a will that wants the good and simultaneously wants to go on wanting otherwise.

column1: What did the "books of the Platonists" give Augustine that Manichaeism could not, and what did they fail to give him?
column2: The Platonists gave him an incorporeal conception of God as Being itself, and the privation account of evil (VII.9–VII.16). They failed to give him humility, incarnation, and grace (VII.18–VII.21).

column1: State the privation theory of evil, and explain how it preserves both God's goodness and human responsibility.
column2: Evil is a privation: a lack, corruption, or disorder in a good nature, as blindness is absence of sight (VII.12–VII.16). God's goodness is preserved because he authors no evil substance; responsibility is preserved because the will's turning toward lower goods is its own act.

column1: In Book VIII, what is the "divided will," and why could Augustine command his body but not his own wanting?
column2: The divided will is one will split against itself: the old will of habit pulling toward the familiar life, the new will of conviction pulling toward continence (VIII.5, VIII.8–VIII.11). He could command his body because the body obeys a single command; he could not command his wanting because the command itself was divided.

column1: What role do the stories of Victorinus and Antony play in Augustine's conversion, and how do they differ from the theater's effect in Book III?
column2: Victorinus (VIII.2) and Antony, via Ponticianus (VIII.6), show that the life Augustine wants is actually being lived, by people no better equipped than himself. The theater (III.2) moved his emotions without moving his will; these examples move his will.

column1: What happened in the garden (VIII.12), and why does Augustine present the conversion as healing rather than as a change of belief?
column2: In the garden he heard a child's voice chanting "take up and read," opened Romans, and read the injunction to put on Christ (VIII.12; Romans 13:13–14). He presents it as healing because his beliefs were already formed; what changed was the will, made whole by grace working through an external occasion.

column1: Why is the question "what was God doing before creation?" a mistake, on Augustine's account?
column2: Time was created with the world, not before it (XI.10–XI.13). "Before" creation assumes a time in which God waited; but eternity is a timeless present, and creation includes time itself, so the question rests on a false presupposition.

column1: Explain the threefold present (XI.20) and the example of the recited psalm (XI.27–XI.28).
column2: The threefold present (XI.20): the present of past things is memory, of present things attention, of future things expectation. Reciting a psalm (XI.27–XI.28), expectation of the whole drains through attention, syllable by syllable, into memory; the passage measured is the soul's distension across the three.

column1: How does Book XI's theory of time connect with Book I's claim about restlessness?
column2: Book XI restates Book I as a philosophy of time. The soul distended across past and future is the restless heart in temporal form; its gathering into God's eternal present is the rest it sought from the first sentence.

column1: Why does Augustine say the will's evil movement has no efficient cause, and what problem does that claim create?
column2: An evil will is a deficient movement, a turning away, and a deficiency has no efficient cause the way a positive act does — nothing makes the will turn except the will itself. The problem this creates is explanatory: if there is no cause, the turning looks unintelligible.

column1: Augustine says God is found by turning inward. Does that make his God merely a feature of the soul? Give the strongest reason on each side.
column2: For the "merely interior" reading: the vision of Book VII is reported as an experience of the soul, and everything Augustine cites as evidence is inward. Against it: Augustine insists the Being encountered is above the soul, not a part of it — present within, but unchangeable where the soul is changeable.

column1: Why does Beauvoir say the question "What is a woman?" cannot be answered by biology alone, or by appealing to the "eternal feminine"?
column2: Biology describes a body, not a destiny: nothing in pregnancy or sexual dimorphism entails exclusion from public life or the experience of oneself as a relative being. The eternal feminine explains nothing: it restates the mystery — that women are somehow essentially this way — as if it were an answer.

column1: What does Beauvoir mean by woman as the Other, and how does her otherness differ from that of other oppressed groups?
column2: Woman as Other means she is constituted as the inessential counterpart against whom man defines himself as Subject and Absolute. Her otherness differs from other oppressed groups because she does not stand over against men as a separate group; she lives dispersed among them, without a shared past, religion, or institutions of her own.

column1: Why does Beauvoir argue that women's dispersion among men makes their subordination unusually durable?
column2: Dispersion blocks solidarity: without a separate collective, a shared history, or institutions of their own, women cannot easily forge the group consciousness through which oppressed groups typically resist — and they share the fortunes of their fathers and husbands rather than the fortunes of women as such.

column1: State Beauvoir's objection to biological explanations of woman's situation in one sentence.
column2: Biology gives a condition, not a cause: the body is an element of woman's situation, but no physiological fact entails the social meanings and limits built on it.

column1: What is her objection to psychoanalysis — what does it describe well, and what does it mistake?
column2: Psychoanalysis describes well how a child experiences her situation — the feelings, conflicts, and identifications of growing up as a girl. It mistakes that experience for a law of the psyche, taking the patriarchal situation as given instead of explaining it.

column1: What does historical materialism explain about woman's situation, and where does Beauvoir say it fails?
column2: Historical materialism explains the economics of dependence: private property and the division of labor made women economically dependent on men. It fails because women's subordination predates private property in the form the theory needs and survives where property relations change — economics is a dimension, not the whole.

column1: What is a "situation" in Beauvoir's sense, and how does it apply — and criticize — the thesis that existence precedes essence?
column2: A situation is a human freedom located in a body and a world, whose possibilities are shaped — opened and closed — by the civilization around it. It applies existence precedes essence because woman has no fixed essence; it criticizes the thesis because freedom is never exercised in a vacuum, and its conditions are unequal.

column1: What is the difference between transcendence and immanence, and why is the distinction central to the book?
column2: Transcendence is the reach beyond the given: projects, creation, risk. Immanence is existence confined to repetition and maintenance. The distinction is central because Beauvoir's charge is that women have been systematically confined to immanence while transcendence is reserved to men — and then blamed for the narrowness the confinement produces.

column1: What does Beauvoir mean by "complicity," and why does she insist on it rather than treating women as pure victims?
column2: Complicity means women partly maintain the order that subordinates them, because surrendering freedom is tempting: immanence is safe, freedom is risky, and the role of the Other brings real advantages. Beauvoir insists on it to refuse both pictures — pure victimhood, which denies freedom, and free choice, which denies situation.

column1: What is the role of the doll in the childhood chapter, and what does it show about how femininity is formed?
column2: The doll teaches identification with a passive object: where a boy's toys invite action on the world, the doll invites the girl to dress, admire, and look at something — and thereby to experience herself as something to be looked at. It shows femininity being formed through the body and play long before any explicit teaching.

column1: Why is puberty a crisis for the young girl in Beauvoir's account, and how does it differ from the boy's puberty?
column2: Puberty is a crisis because the girl's body becomes flesh — heavy, bleeding, exposed to the gaze of others — and is read by others as her meaning, announcing a destiny independent of her will. The boy's puberty confirms his growing power; the girl's announces her object-status.

column1: What are the three escapes the young girl turns to, and what do they prefigure in Volume II?
column2: Narcissism (making her own image her project), love (investing a man with absolute value), and mysticism (addressing absolute devotion to God). They prefigure Volume II's justifications chapters — the narcissist, the woman in love, and the mystic as settled adult strategies.

column1: In what sense is "becomes a woman" a claim about formation rather than about choice — and why does the girl's resistance support, rather than undermine, the claim?
column2: Formation, not choice, because the roads are closed before she chooses: her body as others treat it, her education, and the marriage market progressively narrow her future while offering rewards for the open road. Her resistance supports the claim because a nature would not need to be enforced — protest and envy of her brother's freedom show the formation is imposed, not innate.

column1: What does the chapter on the lesbian show about Beauvoir's method, and why is it a useful control case?
column2: The lesbian chapter is a control case: it treats lesbian existence as one possible response to the same situation — a refusal of the feminine destiny shaped by the conditions it refuses — without pathologizing it or simply celebrating it. It shows the method working on a case that fits neither the usual condemnation nor the usual celebration.

column1: Why does Beauvoir argue that economic independence is necessary but not sufficient for liberation, and what else does liberation require?
column2: Economic independence is necessary because a woman who cannot support herself cannot be free. It is not sufficient because work alone, inside a civilization that still constitutes her as Other, leaves her torn between two worlds. Liberation also requires a moral transformation: men and women recognizing each other as equals and subjects, with transcendence open to both.

column1: What is the difference between methodic doubt and skepticism as a conclusion, and which does Descartes practice?
column2: Methodic doubt is a procedure; skepticism is a conclusion. Descartes suspends beliefs that admit of doubt in order to find a foundation, not because he holds that nothing can be known. The book's trajectory — from doubt to God to the external world — is an anti-skeptical project.

column1: The dream argument targets which class of beliefs, and what, if anything, does Descartes think survives it?
column2: The dream argument targets beliefs about the present environment — that you are sitting by a fire, holding paper, and so on. What survives, Descartes suggests, are the simplest general elements out of which both waking and dreaming experience are composed: extension, shape, quantity, number. These are like the colors on a painter's palette.

column1: Why does Descartes introduce the evil demon after the dream argument — what does the demon threaten that dreaming does not?
column2: The demon threatens reason itself. Dreaming casts doubt on the senses and on particular present experiences, but arithmetic and geometry seem to hold even in dreams. The demon hypothesis extends doubt to those: a supremely powerful deceiver could make you go wrong even when you judge that two and three make five.

column1: State the cogito in Descartes's Meditation II formulation, and explain why its scope is limited to the moment of thinking.
column2: I am, I exist, is necessarily true whenever it is put forward by me or conceived in my mind (Cottingham trans.). Its scope is momentary: it secures existence only while the thinking occurs. It does not prove persistence through time, a body, a past, or anything else.

column1: In the wax passage, what changes and what stays the same — and what does Descartes conclude from this about how bodies are known?
column2: Everything sensory changes — taste, smell, color, shape, hardness, sound — while the wax remains the same wax. Descartes concludes that what we know of the wax is not delivered by the senses but grasped by the intellect: the wax as an extended, flexible, changeable thing. Bodies are known by the mind, not the senses.

column1: What does Descartes mean by "objective reality" and "formal reality," and how does the distinction do work in Meditation III?
column2: Objective reality is the reality a thing has as represented in an idea; formal reality is the reality a thing has by existing in its own right. The distinction lets Descartes argue that an idea with infinite objective reality (the idea of God) needs a cause with infinite formal reality — and only God qualifies.

column1: State the causal principle behind the Third Meditation's proof of God, and name its most vulnerable premise.
column2: The causal principle: there must be at least as much reality in the cause as in the effect; in particular, the objective reality of an idea must be caused by something with at least as much formal reality. Its most vulnerable premise is the principle itself — the claim that "degrees of reality" behave like quantities a cause must match is a piece of scholastic metaphysics most modern readers reject.

column1: Why, on Descartes's account, can the idea of God not be derived by negating my own finitude?
column2: Negation yields only "not-finite," not the positive content of infinity. And Descartes argues the order runs the other way: I recognize my own defects and finitude only by comparison with a prior idea of perfection, so the idea of perfection cannot be derived from the finite mind it is used to judge.

column1: How does Meditation IV reconcile a perfect, non-deceiving God with the fact that I make errors?
column2: Error is my misuse of good faculties, not a defect in them. The intellect is finite; the will is effectively unlimited in scope. Error occurs when the will judges about matters the intellect does not clearly and distinctly perceive. God gave faculties that, used within their limits, do not err; the fault lies in my free assent beyond those limits.

column1: What is the Cartesian circle, who raised it, and what is the strongest reply to it?
column2: The circle: Descartes seems to prove God using clear and distinct perceptions, then to validate clear and distinct perceptions by God's non-deceptive nature. It was raised by Antoine Arnauld in the Fourth Objections. The strongest reply, on most readings, is the memory reply: only remembered clear and distinct perceptions need God's guarantee, while present intuitions are self-certifying — though critics object that the proof of God itself takes time and relies on memory.

column1: How does the Fifth Meditation's ontological argument differ from the Third Meditation's causal argument?
column2: The Third Meditation argues from the cause of an idea (only God could cause the idea of an infinite being in a finite mind). The Fifth argues from the content of the idea (existence belongs to the idea of a supremely perfect being as necessarily as three-sidedness belongs to a triangle). The Third is causal and a posteriori in form; the Fifth is conceptual and a priori.

column1: State the real distinction argument in one paragraph, and explain why it generates the interaction problem.
column2: The real distinction argument: I clearly and distinctly conceive mind as thinking and unextended, and body as extended and unthinking; what I can clearly and distinctly conceive as separate, God can separate; therefore mind and body are really distinct substances. It generates the interaction problem because two substances with nothing in common — one unextended, one extended — seem to lack any mechanism of causal contact, yet experience shows them interacting constantly.

column1: In Meditation VI, how does Descartes argue from the passivity of sensation to the existence of material things?
column2: Sensory ideas arrive unbidden and involuntarily — I cannot choose what I seem to see when I open my eyes. The cause cannot be my own mind (the ideas are not produced at will) and cannot be God directly (a non-deceiving God would not give me a powerful natural inclination to believe bodies cause them if they did not). So material things exist as their cause.

column1: Why does Descartes reject the image of the mind as a pilot in a ship?
column2: Because the pilot is merely lodged in the ship, not united with it. Descartes insists the mind is intermingled with the body, so that sensations — pain, hunger, thirst — are not mere observations of damage but confused thoughts arising from the union, teaching the composite being what helps or harms it. A pilot would merely see the ship's damage; a mind feels its body's pain.

column1: State the two documents of the opening pages, their dates, and the question Foucault sets by juxtaposing them.
column2: The two documents are Damiens's public execution in Paris in 1757 and Léon Faucher's timetable for a Paris house of young prisoners, dated 1838. Foucault's question: what changed — in object, technology, and reach — between a spectacular killing on the body and a silent schedule ordering a whole day?

column1: Why is humanitarian progress not, for Foucault, a sufficient explanation of the change from scaffold to timetable?
column2: Humanitarianism is insufficient because it explains at most why punishment became less terrible; it does not explain the replacement's form — detailed knowledge of offenders, continuous training, timetables, surveillance across many institutions. The new power is milder in means and more thorough in grip; an explanation must cover both.

column1: In the classical regime, why was a crime an offense against the sovereign, and what two functions did public execution perform?
column2: A crime offended the sovereign because the law resided in the sovereign's person, so every offense injured his power as well as its victim. Public execution performed an epistemic function — displaying the crime's truth, crowned by confession — and a political function: restoring the sovereign's wounded power on the condemned body.

column1: What made the spectacle of the scaffold politically risky for the power that staged it?
column2: The spectacle was risky because it required the crowd's participation, and the crowd could refuse: pitying or heroising the condemned, turning the last speech against authority, resenting the executioner, or rioting. A power staging itself through a crowd builds inversion into its central ritual.

column1: What did the eighteenth-century reformers propose instead of torture, and in what sense did their program aim at the "soul" and at representation?
column2: The reformers proposed legality, proportionality, and a semiotics of punishment: fixed laws, penalties representing the crime and advertising its disadvantage, prevention over vengeance, useful public work. It aimed at the soul because its target was representations in citizens' and offenders' minds — the imagined calculus of crime and penalty — not pain on the body.

column1: Define a docile body, and name the four families of techniques by which discipline produces one.
column2: A docile body can be subjected, used, transformed, and improved — made more capable and more obedient by the same operations. The four techniques: art of distributions (space), control of activity (time and movement), organization of geneses (graded development), composition of forces (combining bodies into an efficient whole).

column1: Give one example each of the art of distributions, the control of activity, the organization of geneses, and the composition of forces.
column2: Distributions: each pupil assigned a fixed, ranked classroom place. Control of activity: a timetable prescribing the timed sequence and posture of an act, as in drill or handwriting. Geneses: a curriculum divided into graded stages, each closed by a test. Composition of forces: trained bodies arranged into a platoon, class, or line whose combined force exceeds the sum of its parts.

column1: What are the three means of correct training, and why is the third the most important of them?
column2: The three means are hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment, and the examination. The examination matters most because it combines the other two: it observes, compares against a norm, and turns the person into a documented case — where power produces both individuality and knowledge of individuals.

column1: Explain the formula that normalizing judgment homogenises while individualizing.
column2: Normalizing judgment homogenises by pressing everyone toward one standard; it individualizes by measuring and recording each person's particular gap from that standard — the specific lateness, weakness, or deviation that makes this individual the object of correction.

column1: How does the Panopticon make power automatic, and what does "visible and unverifiable" mean?
column2: The Panopticon makes power automatic because the inmate, in a backlit cell facing a tower he cannot see into, must assume he may be watched at any moment and so watches himself; it works whoever — or no one — is in the tower. Visible: the tower is constantly before his eyes. Unverifiable: he can never confirm whether the gaze is on him now.

column1: What is the difference between the Panopticon as a building and the panoptic schema as a diagram — and why does the distinction matter for Foucault's claim?
column2: As a building, the Panopticon is Bentham's circular design, rarely constructed. As a diagram, the panoptic schema is the abstract mechanism — distribution, visibility, individualizing records — adaptable to schools, hospitals, and factories. Foucault's claim is the diagram's diffusion, so the scarcity of circular prisons does not touch it.

column1: Contrast the leper and the plague town as two models of power, and say how Foucault thinks the nineteenth century combined them.
column2: The leper models power by exclusion: casting out the impure. The plague town models power by disciplinary inclusion: quarantine, registration, daily inspection, minute recording of everyone in place. The nineteenth century combined them: categories marked off as abnormal are simultaneously subjected to detailed disciplinary management.

column1: What is delinquency, as distinct from crime, and in what senses is its production useful?
column2: Delinquency is not crime in general but the penal system's product: a documented milieu of habitual offenders — the delinquent as a type, with biography and predicted future — manufactured by imprisonment, stigma, records, and post-release supervision. It is useful because a known milieu can be watched and infiltrated, it separates criminalised poverty from better-tolerated illegalities, and it legitimises supervision beyond the prison.

column1: What is the carceral continuum, and what does Foucault's claim that the prison resembles factories, schools, barracks, and hospitals mean?
column2: The carceral continuum is the graduated network of corrective institutions — prison, reformatory, supervised release, welfare and educational tutelage — across which normalizing judgment extends, so punishment shades into assistance without a sharp boundary. The resemblance claim means these institutions share techniques — enclosure, timetables, observation, examination — not that a school is morally a jail.

column1: State the two poles of biopower and the contrast between "make die and let live" and "make live and let die."
column2: Biopower's poles are the anatomo-politics of the human body (disciplines training individual bodies) and the biopolitics of the population (regulation of births, mortality, health, life expectancy). "Make die and let live" is sovereign power, whose essence is the right to kill; "make live and let die" is biopower, which fosters and administers life and lets die by neglect or exclusion.

column1: What does Hobbes mean by "equality" in chapter 13, and why does it matter that even the weakest can kill the strongest?
column2: Equality means no one is so far above the rest that they can count on prevailing: even the weakest can kill the strongest by stealth or alliance. It matters because it removes the escape route of natural superiority — no one is safe by being strong, so everyone faces the same insecurity.

column1: Name the three causes of quarrel.
column2: Competition (gain), diffidence (safety), and glory (reputation).

column1: What does Hobbes mean when he says the state of nature is a condition of "war," if he does not mean constant fighting?
column2: War means a known disposition to fight over a tract of time, as bad weather means a disposition to foulness, not perpetual rain. Actual fighting may be intermittent; what defines the condition is that no one can count on peace.

column1: State the distinction between a right of nature and a law of nature, and explain why Hobbes says they differ as liberty differs from obligation.
column2: A right of nature is the liberty to use one's power as one will for self-preservation — in the state of nature, a right to all things. A law of nature is a precept of reason forbidding what destroys life or omitting what preserves it. They differ as liberty (absence of obligation) differs from obligation (a bond on action).

column1: State the first and second laws of nature, and explain how the second follows from the first.
column2: First law: seek peace as far as peace can be had; otherwise use the advantages of war. Second law: lay down your right to all things when others will do the same, keeping only as much liberty as you allow others. The second follows because peace is impossible while everyone retains an unlimited right to everything, including each other's bodies.

column1: Why, on Hobbes's account, are covenants made in the state of nature void in practice whenever reasonable suspicion arises?
column2: Because keeping your side alone, when the other party will not keep theirs, is self-destruction — contrary to the reason for covenanting. Words without fear of a coercive power are too weak to bind, so a covenant collapses at the first reasonable suspicion of non-performance.

column1: What is the third law of nature, and how does Hobbes define justice in terms of it?
column2: Third law: perform covenants made. Justice is keeping covenants; injustice is breaking them. Before covenants there is neither just nor unjust, because there is nothing to keep or break.

column1: Reconstruct the Foole's objection and Hobbes's reply, and state one weakness in the reply.
column2: The Foole says there is no justice: breaking a covenant secretly, when it pays, is rational. Hobbes replies that breach adopts a policy of breach, and a person known to break covenants when advantageous cannot be received into any society — destroying their own security, the very thing they sought. Weakness: the reply assumes the breach is known or generalized; a truly secret breach, never discovered, seems to escape it.

column1: Explain the distinction between author, actor, and person in chapter 16, and why a multitude needs a representative to be one person.
column2: A person is one whose words or actions are considered as their own (natural person) or as representing another (artificial person). The author owns the words and actions; the actor performs them by the author's authority. A multitude needs a representative because, without one, it is many persons, not one: only when one person or assembly represents it can it speak and act as a unity.

column1: State the covenant of chapter 17 in your own words, and explain why the sovereign is not a party to it.
column2: The covenant: each person says to each other, in effect, "I authorise and give up my right of governing myself to this man or assembly, on condition you do the same." The sovereign is not a party because the covenant runs between subjects; the sovereign receives authority from it but promises nothing under it, and so cannot breach it.

column1: Why does Hobbes think sovereignty by acquisition carries the same rights as sovereignty by institution?
column2: Because in both cases subjects submit out of fear of violent death, and protection is the ground of obedience: obligation lasts as long as the power to protect lasts. Institution and acquisition differ in how sovereignty arises, not in the rights it carries — a claim scholars debate, since consent under conquest looks thinner than mutual agreement.

column1: From chapter 18, name four rights of the sovereign, and explain why subjects cannot lawfully accuse the sovereign of injustice.
column2: Rights include: sole legislation; judging controversies; making war and peace; choosing counsellors and ministers; judging what doctrines may be publicly taught. Subjects cannot accuse the sovereign of injustice because the sovereign acts by their authority — its acts are their own acts, so accusing it is accusing themselves.

column1: Why does Hobbes say tyranny and oligarchy are not distinct forms of government?
column2: Because tyranny and oligarchy are names of disapproval, not distinct forms: monarchy disliked is called tyranny, aristocracy disliked is called oligarchy. Forms are distinguished by the representative (one, some, all), not by whether the ruler is liked.

column1: What is liberty for Hobbes, and where are subjects free in a commonwealth?
column2: Liberty is the absence of external impediments to motion. Subjects are free where the law is silent: where the sovereign has not legislated, they may act as they judge best. Liberty is thus a space left by law, not a moral power against it.

column1: What rights does a subject retain under chapter 21, and why does the retained right of self-preservation not amount to a right of revolution?
column2: Subjects retain the liberty to resist immediate violence to their body, refuse self-destruction or self-wounding, refuse self-incrimination without pardon, and disobey commands endangering their life. This is not a right of revolution because it is individual and defensive: it licenses no collective judgment, no deposition, and no standing mechanism against the sovereign — only refusal in the extreme case where obedience would defeat the covenant's purpose, preservation.

column1: What is the difference between "easy" and "abstruse" philosophy in Section I, and which does Hume favor?
column2: Easy philosophy treats of common life and manners, pleases taste, and reforms conduct; "abstruse" philosophy aims at precise, systematic knowledge of human nature but risks obscurity. Hume wants an accurate philosophy that is also accessible — he criticizes abstruse metaphysics when it becomes unintelligible, not precision itself.

column1: State the copy principle, and explain why Hume raises the case of the missing shade of blue.
column2: Every simple idea is copied from a corresponding simple impression. The missing shade of blue is Hume's own counterexample: someone who has seen all other shades could form the idea of the missing one without an impression. Hume concedes it but calls it too singular to overturn the principle.

column1: What are the three principles of association of ideas, and which one matters most for the rest of the book?
column2: Resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect. Cause and effect matters most, because Sections IV–VII analyze causal inference, which operates through association and custom.

column1: What is Hume's fork, and why does the denial of a relation of ideas imply a contradiction while the denial of a matter of fact does not?
column2: Relations of ideas (mathematics, logic) are demonstratively certain; denying one implies a contradiction. Matters of fact are known only by experience, and their contrary is always conceivable without contradiction — a world where the sun does not rise tomorrow is thinkable.

column1: In Section IV, why can the uniformity principle ("the future will resemble the past") not be proved by demonstration?
column2: Demonstration establishes what cannot be otherwise without contradiction. A changed course of nature involves no contradiction, so the uniformity principle cannot be demonstrated.

column1: Why can it not be proved by experience either? What is the circularity Hume alleges?
column2: Experiential reasoning itself presupposes uniformity: to argue from past experience to future uniformity is to assume that the past is a guide to the future, which is the very principle in question. The argument is circular.

column1: What does Hume mean by the "sceptical solution" in Section V, and how does custom solve — and fail to solve — the problem of induction?
column2: The skeptical solution concedes that induction has no rational foundation, but explains that custom or habit — the mind's determination after repeated conjunction — is what actually carries us from past to future. It solves the psychological question (why do we infer?) but not the justificatory one (what warrants the inference?).

column1: In Section VII, why does Hume reject the suggestion that the idea of necessity comes from reflection on the will's power over the body?
column2: The will's power over the body is itself known only through experience of constant conjunction, and its mechanism is unknown to us; it therefore cannot supply an original impression of power or necessity. Appealing to it would presuppose what is to be explained.

column1: Give Hume's two definitions of cause. Why might they seem to be in tension?
column2: (1) An object followed by another, where all similar objects are followed by similar objects (regularity). (2) An object whose appearance conveys the mind, by custom, to the idea of the other (the mind's transition). They may seem in tension because the first locates causation in objects and their regularities, the second in the mind's habitual movement — whether Hume intended them as equivalent or complementary is debated.

column1: What does Hume mean by "liberty" in Section VIII, and why does he think necessity is required for moral responsibility?
column2: Liberty is "a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will" — freedom from external constraint, not from causation. Necessity is required for moral responsibility because an action unconnected with character and motives would reveal nothing about the agent and could not be praised or blamed.

column1: Why does Hume discuss animals in Section IX? What work is the section doing in the book's overall argument?
column2: Animals learn from experience — a dog avoids fire, expects food at a familiar sound — without any rational faculty. This confirms that human causal inference is likewise the work of custom and instinct, not of reason, and supports the naturalism of Section V.

column1: State Hume's maxim about testimony and miracles. Does his argument show that miracles cannot occur? Why or why not?
column2: No testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish. No: the argument concerns whether testimony can rationally warrant belief in a miracle, not whether miracles are possible.

column1: In Section XI, why does Hume argue that reason cannot establish a future state of rewards and punishments from the observed world?
column2: Reason can infer a cause only in proportion to its observed effects. The world as observed is mixed and imperfect, so it does not warrant inferring a perfectly just and benevolent governor or a future state designed to redress earthly injustice; those attributes go beyond what the effect shows.

column1: What is the difference between Pyrrhonian and Academic (mitigated) skepticism in Section XII, and why does Hume say the former is unliveable?
column2: Pyrrhonian skepticism is total doubt, which Hume says nature makes unliveable — we cannot sustain it outside the study. Academic or mitigated skepticism accepts skeptical arguments but confines them: it doubts abstruse speculation, limits enquiry to what human understanding can handle, and recommends modesty, while leaving common life untouched.

column1: What do A and B in a citation such as A51/B75 refer to, and which text should you read where both exist?
column2: A = the first edition (1781), B = the second, revised edition (1787), cited by original page numbers. Read B where both exist; keep the A Deduction as the famous alternative route.

column1: State the Copernican analogy in the B Preface. What exactly is being reversed?
column2: As Copernicus explained the heavens better by moving the observer, objects of experience conform to our cognition rather than cognition to objects — a reversal about the form of experience.

column1: Distinguish analytic/synthetic and a priori/a posteriori. Why is "synthetic a priori" a problem?
column2: Analytic: the predicate is contained in the subject. Synthetic: it adds something. A priori: independent of particular experience, necessary and strictly universal; a posteriori: resting on experience. Synthetic a priori judgments extend knowledge yet hold necessarily — neither unpacking nor experience seems able to supply both features.

column1: What question does the Introduction pose as the Critique's driving question, and what is Kant's one-sentence answer to it?
column2: How are synthetic a priori judgments possible? They articulate the structure our faculties contribute to experience, so they hold necessarily of everything experienceable — and of nothing else.

column1: Give two of Kant's arguments that space is an a priori intuition rather than an empirical concept.
column2: Any two of: space is presupposed, not derived (representing things as outside me already requires space); space is necessary (empty space is representable, an outer object outside space is not); space is a single infinite intuition, not a general concept.

column1: What does it mean to call space and time "transcendentally ideal but empirically real"?
column2: Transcendentally ideal: space and time belong to our mode of cognition, not to things apart from it. Empirically real: within experience they are fully objective — public, measurable, law-governed, not private or illusory.

column1: State the two-world (two-object) and two-aspect readings of the phenomena / things-in-themselves distinction.
column2: Two-world: phenomena and things in themselves are two distinct realms of objects. Two-aspect: one world, considered two ways — as it appears under our cognitive conditions, and in abstraction from them. The dispute is unresolved; this guide takes no side.

column1: What are the categories, and what work does the Metaphysical Deduction claim to do?
column2: The categories are the understanding's twelve pure concepts — a priori rules for unifying a manifold into experience of objects. The Metaphysical Deduction claims to derive them completely and systematically from the forms of judgment.

column1: What does "the I think must be able to accompany all my representations" mean, and what is its role in the Deduction?
column2: Every representation of mine must in principle be capable of being taken up into one self-consciousness. This unity of apperception is the Deduction's supreme premise, from which the categories' validity is derived.

column1: State the Deduction's conclusion, including its built-in limit.
column2: The categories apply necessarily to all objects of possible experience. The limit: they yield knowledge only where intuition can be given, and are empty forms of thought beyond it.

column1: What problem does the Schematism solve, and what is Kant's mediator?
column2: The problem of application: pure, non-sensible concepts must apply to sensible appearances. Kant's mediator is the schema — a determination of time according to a category's rule.

column1: In the Paralogisms, what slide does Kant accuse rational psychology of making?
column2: Rational psychology slides from a formal feature of thought to a property of a thing: from the "I" as logical subject, and consciousness's unity and identity, it infers a soul that is a simple, persisting substance.

column1: State the First Antinomy's thesis, antithesis, and Kant's resolution. How does the Third's resolution differ in form?
column2: First Antinomy: thesis, the world has a beginning in time and spatial limits; antithesis, it is infinite in both. Resolution: both false — the world as completed totality is not an object given in itself. The Third resolves differently: both can be true, from different standpoints.

column1: What does the Third Antinomy establish about freedom — and what does it not establish?
column2: It establishes that freedom is thinkable without contradiction alongside universal natural causality. It does not establish that we are free; that question passes to practical reason, as in the Groundwork's Section 3.

column1: State Kant's three questions. How does the Canon answer "What may I hope?"
column2: What can I know? What ought I to do? What may I hope? The Canon answers the third through the highest good: if I do what I ought, I may hope for happiness proportioned to worthiness — rational only as faith, never as knowledge.

column1: What does Kant mean by saying that nothing is good without limitation except a good will, and why does he think wealth or intelligence fails that test?
column2: Only the good will is good without limitation (4:393–394) because everything else — intelligence, courage, wealth, happiness — can be misused or can corrupt its possessor; its goodness depends on the will directing it. A good will is good by its willing alone, whatever it achieves.

column1: What is the difference between acting in conformity with duty and acting from duty, and why does Kant think only the second has moral worth?
column2: Acting in conformity with duty matches what duty requires but from another motive, such as profit; acting from duty is done from respect for the moral law itself. Only the second has moral worth, because only it would remain if the incentives changed.

column1: What is a maxim, and why does Kant's moral theory test maxims rather than acts in the abstract?
column2: A maxim is the subjective principle of an act — roughly, in circumstances of this kind, I will do this, for this purpose. Kant tests maxims because the same outward act can be done on different principles, and moral evaluation concerns the principle the agent acts on.

column1: What is the difference between a hypothetical imperative and a categorical imperative, and why must morality take the second form?
column2: A hypothetical imperative binds conditionally: if you want an end, take the means. A categorical imperative commands unconditionally, regardless of your wants. Morality must take the categorical form, since a morality binding only those who happened to want something would not be unconditional.

column1: State the formula of universal law. What are the two ways a maxim can fail its test?
column2: Act only in accordance with that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law (4:421). A maxim fails by contradiction in conception (it cannot even be conceived as a universal law) or by contradiction in the will (it can be conceived but cannot be willed by a rational being).

column1: Apply the universal-law formula to the lying-promise case: why does the maxim defeat itself when universalized?
column2: The lying promise (4:422) universalized destroys promising: if everyone borrowed on false promises when short of money, promises would no longer be believed, so the liar's own maxim could not succeed. The maxim exploits a practice it would destroy.

column1: In the four illustrations, which cases does Kant present as perfect duties and which as imperfect duties, and what is the difference between those two kinds of duty?
column2: Perfect duties: not committing suicide and not making lying promises — duties admitting no exception. Imperfect duties: developing one's talents and helping others — duties of a kind that leave latitude about when and how they are fulfilled.

column1: State the formula of humanity. What does Kant mean by "humanity," and what is the difference between using someone as a means and using them merely as a means?
column2: Act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end and never merely as a means (4:429). Humanity means rational nature, the capacity to set ends. Using someone as a means is ordinary — employing their services — but using them merely as a means bypasses their rational consent and treats them as a tool only.

column1: Why does Kant think deception and coercion are paradigm violations of the humanity formula?
column2: Deception and coercion work by circumventing rational agency: the deceived person acts on a belief deliberately created for them, and the coerced person is compelled rather than persuaded. Both bypass the consent that treating someone as an end requires.

column1: State the formula of autonomy and the formula of the kingdom of ends. How are they related?
column2: Autonomy (4:431): the will of every rational being gives universal law to itself. The kingdom of ends (4:433): a systematic union of rational beings, each an end, under self-given common laws — autonomy made social.

column1: What is heteronomy, and why does Kant charge all previous moral theories with it?
column2: Heteronomy is a will whose law comes from outside reason — inclination, authority, happiness, or externally imposed divine command. Kant charges previous theories with heteronomy because they grounded obligation somewhere other than the will's own lawgiving.

column1: In §3, what does Kant mean by saying a free will and a will under moral laws are one and the same?
column2: A free will is one determined by nothing alien to it; a will determined by nothing alien is determined by a law it gives itself; and a law a rational will gives itself universally is the moral law (4:447). Freedom and subjection to moral law are therefore the same property viewed two ways.

column1: What is the circularity problem in §3, and how does Kant's distinction between two standpoints attempt to answer it?
column2: The circle (4:450): freedom is assumed to derive morality, and morality is then appealed to in order to establish freedom. Kant's answer is the two standpoints (4:451–453): as a phenomenon I am determined, as an intelligence I must regard myself as free, and practical deliberation requires the second standpoint.

column1: What is the difference between the analytic route of §§1–2 and the synthetic route of §3?
column2: The analytic route (§§1–2) ascends from ordinary moral cognition to the supreme principle. The synthetic route (§3) descends from the principle back to ordinary cognition, asking whether it genuinely binds beings like us.

column1: Why does Kant say we cannot explain how freedom is possible, and what does he offer instead of such an explanation?
column2: We cannot explain how freedom is possible because explanation would trace it to causes in the world of sense, where freedom by definition does not operate (4:458–463). What Kant offers instead is a practical vindication: we must act under the idea of freedom, and that standpoint suffices for morality's authority.

column1: How does the Groundwork's §3 argument relate to the third antinomy of the Critique of Pure Reason, as summarized in this guide's closing section?
column2: The third antinomy shows theoretical reason can prove both determinism and freedom, and therefore neither — a stalemate. Section 3 presupposes that stalemate: since theory cannot settle freedom, the question is handed to practical reason, which requires us to act under the idea of freedom.

column1: In chapter 1, what is the disquieting suggestion, and what work does the taboo analogy do?
column2: The disquieting suggestion: moral language is in the state science's would be after catastrophe and fragmentary revival — fragments of older schemes, used without the whole that made them intelligible. The taboo analogy exhibits a real case — a term surviving the practice that gave it sense — as a model for virtue, duty, and rights.

column1: State the three characteristics of contemporary moral debate from chapter 2, and explain how the third qualifies the second.
column2: The three characteristics: (i) interminability — no rational procedure settles the debates; (ii) conceptual incommensurability — rival, individually valid arguments invoke rival concepts, with no shared weighing standard; (iii) the purported appeal to impersonal rational criteria. The third qualifies the second because the incommensurability is masked — premises descend from different historical sources, so the impersonal tribunal is an illusion.

column1: What is emotivism, and in what precise sense does MacIntyre say it is true while also saying it is false?
column2: Emotivism holds all moral judgments to be nothing but expressions of preference, attitude, or feeling — neither true nor false. It is true as sociology: it describes how moral utterances are used in our culture, to express attitude and manipulate others. It is false as a theory of meaning: expressing feeling is a function of a sentence's use, not its meaning, and emotivism cannot distinguish expressing approval from passing judgment.

column1: What is a "character" in MacIntyre's technical sense, and what does each of the Manager, the Therapist, and the Aesthete embody?
column2: A character is a social role embodying a culture's norms — a fusion of social type and moral exemplar. The Manager: bureaucratic authority claiming means–ends expertise. The Therapist: technique applied to private life, adjusting persons to given ends. The Aesthete: consumption of experience, others as means to aesthetic interest. All replace moral argument with manipulation or taste.

column1: Describe the threefold teleological scheme, and state why discarding its middle term made the Enlightenment project incoherent.
column2: The threefold scheme: man-as-he-happens-to-be; man-as-he-could-be-if-he-realized-his-essential-nature (the telos); and the precepts as the bridge between them. Discarding the middle term left precepts designed to transform human nature with only untutored nature to found them on; precepts whose point was correction cannot be derived from what they exist to correct.

column1: Give MacIntyre's reasons for the failure of each foundation: the passions (Hume), reason (Kant), radical choice (Kierkegaard), utility (Mill).
column2: Passions (Hume): passions conflict, and choosing which shall rule needs a criterion outside them; Hume's choices smuggle in his order's standards. Reason (Kant): universalizability is a formal test immoral maxims can pass, and cannot generate the inherited content. Radical choice (Kierkegaard): a criterionless choice confers no authority. Utility (Mill): "the greatest happiness" is not one measurable quantity; pleasures differ in kind, the calculus has no unit.

column1: Why, in chapters 7–8, is the Manager's claim to expertise a fiction — what would social science have to be like for it to stand?
column2: Managerial expertise would require law-like social-scientific generalizations with predictive power. Chapter 8 argues these systematically fail — radical innovation is unpredictable in principle, knowledge of predictions changes outcomes, contingency intervenes — so the Manager's authority rests on knowledge nobody possesses.

column1: State the fork of chapter 9, and MacIntyre's reason for denying that Nietzsche's critique touches the Aristotelian tradition in its strong form.
column2: The fork: either follow Nietzsche — morality unmasked as will to power, values created by sovereign self-assertion — or recover Aristotle. Nietzsche's critique demolishes only the Enlightenment's fragments; against the Aristotelian tradition in its strong form the unmasking has no purchase, while Nietzsche's alternative presupposes the inheritances it claims to transcend.

column1: Define a practice, and distinguish internal from external goods using the chess example.
column2: A practice is a coherent, complex, socially established cooperative activity with standards of excellence partly definitive of it, through which goods internal to it are realized. In the chess example, the sweets bribing a child to play are an external good — obtainable many ways, competitively possessed; the analytical skill and strategic imagination later found in chess itself are internal goods — achievable only through the practice, fully recognisable only by participants, and enriching the whole community of players.

column1: What are institutions, and why are they both necessary to practices and a standing threat to them?
column2: Institutions — clubs, universities, hospitals, firms — house practices, distributing the external goods they need to survive. They threaten them because their logic is external goods, tending to subordinate internal excellence to revenue, prestige, and survival, unless the virtues resist.

column1: Give MacIntyre's chapter 14 definition of a virtue, and name the three virtues he says practices cannot survive without.
column2: Chapter 14's definition: a virtue is an acquired human quality whose possession and exercise enables us to achieve goods internal to practices, and whose lack prevents us achieving any such goods. The three indispensable virtues: justice, courage, and honesty.

column1: What does it mean to call a human life a narrative quest, and how do intelligibility and accountability follow from the narrative account?
column2: A narrative quest is a life whose unity is that of a story ordered by a search for the good — a good partly understood only through the searching. Intelligibility follows because an action makes sense only located in a life's story and its settings; accountability follows because the agent is that story's subject, answerable to others entitled to demand an account of it.

column1: Define a tradition, and explain how one can rationally defeat a rival without a neutral, tradition-free standard.
column2: A tradition is a historically extended, socially embodied argument, in part about the goods constituting it. It can defeat a rival in epistemological crisis: when it resolves problems its own methods generated but could not solve, and explains — in terms the rival must recognize — why the rival was bound to fail comparably, the defeat is rational without any neutral standpoint. Aquinas is the example.

column1: Why does MacIntyre reject the label "communitarian," and what should he be called instead?
column2: The label is rejected because his is not a political theory of community: he does not propose the modern state embody a shared good (he thinks it cannot), he distrusts political invocations of "community," and his framework is practices, narratives, and traditions ordered to a Thomist human good. He is a Thomist Aristotelian.

column1: What does the closing St. Benedict passage actually propose, and what does it not propose?
column2: St. Benedict proposes constructing local forms of community — ordered to practices, civility, and the moral and intellectual life — within which those goods can survive a dark age. It does not propose capturing the state, restoring a medieval order, or waiting passively: the waiting is a building, and the Benedict is "doubtless very different."

column1: State the harm principle exactly as Mill states it in On Liberty chapter 1, and explain the difference between compulsion and persuasion in his account.
column2: The principle (ch. 1): "the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant." Compulsion is coercion by law or overwhelming social pressure; persuasion — reasoning, remonstrating, entreating — remains always permitted, even for harmless conduct.

column1: Why does Mill say he fears the tyranny of the majority exercised through opinion more than political despotism?
column2: Social tyranny penetrates more deeply into life than political despotism, leaves fewer means of escape (there is no frontier to flee across from opinion), and enforces itself through constant pressure of respectability and custom rather than occasional acts of state power.

column1: In chapter 2, what happens, on Mill's view, when a true opinion is held without understanding its grounds — and why is that a loss?
column2: A true opinion held without understanding its grounds is a dead dogma, not a living belief: repeated as a formula, undefended when challenged, doing no intellectual work. Truth ceases to be understood, and so ceases to guide conduct intelligently.

column1: What are the three cases Mill considers for a silenced opinion, and what does society lose in each?
column2: If true, society loses the chance to exchange error for truth. If false, it loses the collision keeping true belief alive and understood. If partly true (the most common case), it loses the part of the truth the dissenting opinion contains and the received opinion lacks.

column1: Explain the corn-dealer example: why is the same speech protected discussion in one context and punishable instigation in another?
column2: The corn-dealer example turns on context: telling a newspaper reader that corn dealers starve the poor is discussion; telling the same thing to an excited mob outside a corn dealer's house is positive instigation to a mischievous act. The words are the same; what changes is whether speech functions as argument or as trigger to action.

column1: What is an "experiment in living," and why does Mill think society needs experiments it cannot predict the outcome of?
column2: An experiment in living is a new way of life tried by an individual, whose value cannot be known in advance. Society needs such experiments because progress depends on discovering better ways of living than the received ones, and no one can know which will succeed without trying them.

column1: Why does Mill think custom is the enemy of individuality, and what faculties does choosing a life develop?
column2: Custom replaces choice with imitation: people ask what is done, not what suits their character. Choosing develops perception, judgment, discrimination, mental activity, and moral preference — faculties conformity leaves unused, whose exercise is itself part of well-being.

column1: In chapter 4, what duties may society compel a person to perform, and why are those compulsions consistent with the harm principle?
column2: Society may compel a fair share of common burdens, testimony, contribution to the common defense, and children's education. These enforce duties owed to others, not paternalism for the agent's own good.

column1: Give one example from chapter 5 where Mill permits regulation, and one where he forbids it, and explain the principle behind each.
column2: Permitted: regulating drink sales, or punishing drunkenness when it causes harm (e.g. a soldier drunk on duty), because others are affected. Forbidden: prohibiting drinking as such, or criminalising private vice on moral grounds alone, because only the agent's own good is at stake.

column1: State the greatest-happiness principle as Mill states it in Utilitarianism chapter 2. Whose happiness counts, and how?
column2: The greatest-happiness principle: actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse — happiness meaning pleasure and the absence of pain. Everyone's happiness counts equally: the standard is the greatest happiness of all concerned, impartially counted.

column1: What is the "doctrine worthy of swine" objection, and how does the higher/lower pleasures distinction answer it?
column2: The swine objection charges that a pleasure-based ethics reduces human beings to animals. Higher pleasures answer it by distinguishing pleasures of intellect, imagination, feeling, and moral sentiment from mere sensation, and claiming the former are more valuable — so a human life is not best measured by quantity of sensation.

column1: Who counts as a competent judge of pleasures, and why does Mill think their verdict settles questions of quality?
column2: A competent judge has experienced both the higher and the lower pleasure in question. Their verdict settles quality, on Mill's view, because experience of both kinds is the only evidence about which is more valuable — as only someone who has tasted two wines can judge between them.

column1: Why does Mill think utilitarianism does not require us to calculate consequences before every action?
column2: Because mankind has learned general rules from experience — do not lie, do not steal, keep promises — whose observance tends to promote happiness. Follow those rules rather than calculating afresh before every act; calculation is for the rare case, and for the legislator designing rules, not everyday conduct.

column1: In chapter 3, what is the ultimate sanction of utility, and how does Mill's account of conscience differ from a supernatural one?
column2: The ultimate sanction is internal: conscience, the pain of violating an internalized standard and the pleasure of living up to it. Mill's conscience is naturalistic — built by sympathy, education, and association — not a supernatural voice, so it can be educated toward utility rather than merely obeyed.

column1: Reconstruct Mill's "proof" of utility in chapter 4 in three steps, and state Moore's naturalistic-fallacy objection to it.
column2: Three steps: (i) first principles admit no direct proof, only evidence of the kind the subject admits; (ii) the only evidence that something is desirable is that people desire it (as visible is proved by seeing); (iii) each person desires their own happiness, so the general happiness is a good to the aggregate. Moore's objection: the argument slides from "desired" (fact) to "desirable" (value), committing the naturalistic fallacy; "visible" means "can be seen," but "desirable" in a moral argument must mean "ought to be desired."

column1: In chapter 5, why does Mill say security is the most vital of all interests, and how does that explain why rights feel inviolable?
column2: Security is the most vital interest because without assurance that person, property, and expectations will not be arbitrarily violated, no other good can be securely enjoyed.
