Rights feel inviolable because they protect exactly these essential utilities — the groundwork of existence — so violating them threatens the conditions of happiness itself, not merely one pleasure among others.

column1: What question does the Preface say moral philosophers have failed to ask, and what does Nietzsche accuse the "English" moral historians of doing instead?
column2: The unasked question is where morality came from and what it does — its history and function — rather than whether its judgments are true. The "English" historians (Rée and his school) traced morality to utility whose origin was forgotten, but smuggled in the values they claimed to explain, assuming "good" always meant what it means now, and treating morality as one continuous thing with one origin.

column1: What is the difference between the master morality's good/bad distinction and the slave morality's good/evil distinction, and which came first on Nietzsche's account?
column2: Master morality distinguishes good from bad: good means noble, powerful, fine; bad means low, common, wretched — a self-affirmation by the noble, with the contrast secondary. Slave morality distinguishes good from evil: the masters' strength is evil, and the slaves' weakness — meekness, humility, patience — is good. Good/bad came first; good/evil is the product of the slave revolt.

column1: What is ressentiment, and why does Nietzsche say it is creative rather than merely reactive?
column2: Ressentiment is the festering, creative hatred of the powerless, whose reaction is denied outward discharge and ferments inward. It is creative because it does not merely resent: it invents a new value-scheme, redescribing weakness as virtue and strength as vice — an act of spiritual revenge that produces a whole morality.

column1: Explain the lambs-and-birds-of-prey image in Essay I §13: what point is it making about moral judgment?
column2: The lambs judge the birds of prey evil for acting according to their nature, as though the birds had chosen to be predators. Nietzsche's point: the lamb is not morally superior for not being a bird of prey; it simply cannot be one. Slave morality redescribes incapacity as virtue — "I cannot take revenge, therefore I forgive" — and mistakes a difference of nature for a difference of moral worth.

column1: What does Nietzsche mean by "Rome against Judea, Judea against Rome," and who, on his account, won?
column2: Rome embodies noble values; Judea embodies the slave revolt in morals. On Nietzsche's account, Judea won, through Christianity: its inverted values conquered the Roman world and still rule European conscience. The struggle is his compressed history of Western values, not a neutral historical claim, and its details are debated.

column1: What is the "sovereign individual," and why does Nietzsche treat promise-making as an achievement rather than a natural capacity?
column2: The sovereign individual is the person who has acquired, through long discipline, the right to make promises: a proud consciousness of their own reliability, able to hold a future intention against the flux of impulse. Promise-making is an achievement because memory is not natural to human beings — it had to be burned in, by pain, over a long prehistory.

column1: How, on Nietzsche's account, was memory "burned in" to human beings, and what role did pain play?
column2: Memory was burned in by pain: early societies used cruel mnemotechnics — sacrifices, mutilations, bloody rituals — because only what does not cease to hurt stays in the memory. Pain was the only reliable teacher for a creature naturally forgetful.

column1: What is the connection between Schuld (guilt) and debt, and why does Nietzsche insist punishment's purpose is the last thing to learn about it?
column2: Schuld originally meant debt: guilt grew out of the material debtor–creditor relation, where non-payment was compensated by the creditor's pleasure in inflicting suffering. Punishment's purpose is the last thing to learn about it because institutions outlive their origins and acquire new uses — deterrence, reform, retribution are later impositions, not the origin, so present function cannot be read back into origin.

column1: What is bad conscience, and how does Nietzsche explain its origin in the enclosure of human beings in society and the state?
column2: Bad conscience is the soul torturing itself: instincts of cruelty and hostility, blocked from outward discharge when human beings were enclosed in settled society and the state, turned inward — this internalization is the origin of the inner life as self-punishment. The state, on this account, is a cage imposed by force, and bad conscience is the price of civilization.

column1: How does guilt become infinite, on Nietzsche's account, when the debtor–creditor relation is projected onto God?
column2: Guilt becomes infinite when the debtor–creditor relation is projected onto God: humanity owes an unpayable debt to ancestors and gods, and Christianity posits a God who sacrifices himself for that debt — a creditor paying himself — leaving the debtor guilty forever, with a debt that can never be discharged.

column1: In Essay III, what does the ascetic ideal mean for the artist, for the philosopher, and for the priest — and why are the three different?
column2: For the artist, the ascetic ideal means almost nothing — a pose or bridge (Wagner's Parsifal), not a commitment. For the philosopher, it has meant independence: ascetic habits sheltered thinking from the world's noise. For the priest, it is everything: the tool by which suffering is given meaning. The three differ because the same ideal serves different functions for different types.

column1: What is the priest's "genius," on Nietzsche's account, and in what sense is the priest both physician and poisoner?
column2: The priest's genius is giving suffering a meaning by interpreting it as guilt: you suffer because you are sinful. He is a physician because this interpretation keeps the suffering from despairing — meaningless suffering is unbearable — and a poisoner because it teaches self-blame, directs ressentiment inward, and makes the sick sicker even as it keeps them alive.

column1: Why does Nietzsche claim that modern science is the latest form of the ascetic ideal, rather than its refutation?
column2: Science inherits the ascetic structure: its unconditional will to truth treats truth as an absolute value demanding self-sacrifice, a faith that truth is more valuable than life. Science does not refute the ascetic ideal; it is its latest and noblest form, because it preserves the same self-denial in the service of something higher than life.

column1: What does Nietzsche mean by the closing claim that man "would rather will nothingness than not will"?
column2: Man would rather will nothingness than not will means human beings prefer any goal — even self-denial, even nothingness — to goallessness. The ascetic ideal has ruled because it alone gave suffering a meaning; until a rival meaning is created, an ideal that denies life will keep winning over no ideal at all.

column1: State the genetic-fallacy objection to genealogy, and the best reply available to Nietzsche's defenders.
column2: The genetic-fallacy objection: a value's lowly origin does not show it false — a principle discovered through ressentiment might still be right. The best reply: genealogy does not claim origin settles truth; it removes a value's false credential (timeless, divine, disinterested origin) and forces it to be defended on its effects. Genealogy is a clearing operation, not a verdict; Nietzsche's evaluations must be judged on their arguments about what serves life.

column1: How does Nietzsche's master/slave morality differ from Hegel's lordship-and-bondage dialectic, and why does the confusion matter?
column2: Nietzsche's master/slave morality is a typology of value-creation: who creates values, and whether from self-affirmation or reaction. Hegel's lordship and bondage is a dialectic of self-consciousness, in which master and slave are stages in the development of recognition. The confusion matters because it imports Hegel's dialectical resolution — and his account of recognition — into a typology that has neither, and makes Nietzsche's polemic look like a stage in a system it was written against.

column1: Why does Socrates reject Cephalus' definition of justice as telling the truth and returning what one owes?
column2: Cephalus' definition fails on a counterexample (331c–d): returning a weapon to a friend who has gone mad would be truth-telling and debt-repaying, yet would plainly be wrong. Justice cannot be reduced to those two acts.

column1: Polemarchus defines justice as helping friends and harming enemies. What is Socrates' core objection?
column2: Harming cannot improve: justice, as an excellence, cannot make its object worse — medicine heals rather than sickens, and a just person cannot make an enemy worse by harming them (335b–e). The definition also assumes we reliably know who our friends and enemies are, which we often do not.

column1: What does Thrasymachus mean by "the advantage of the stronger," and what is the craft argument Socrates uses against it?
column2: Thrasymachus (338c): each regime makes laws serving its own interest and calls obedience to them "justice." Socrates' craft argument (341c–347e): a craft serves its subject's good, not the practitioner's — medicine serves the patient — so ruling, strictly understood, serves the ruled.

column1: In Glaucon's restatement, what are the three kinds of goods, and in which class must Socrates show justice belongs?
column2: Good in themselves only (e.g. harmless pleasures), good both in themselves and for their consequences (e.g. health, understanding), and good only for their consequences (e.g. medicine, earning money). Socrates must show justice belongs in the second class (357b–358a).

column1: What work does the Ring of Gyges do in Glaucon's challenge?
column2: The Ring of Gyges (359c–360d) tests whether anyone would remain just if injustice carried no penalty: the shepherd, made invisible, seizes power. Glaucon claims everyone would do the same, so justice is kept only from fear of punishment.

column1: Why does Socrates propose to look for justice first in a city rather than in an individual?
column2: The city is justice "written in larger letters" (368c–369a): the structure that is hard to discern in one soul may be easier to see at civic scale, and can then be read back into the individual.

column1: What is the "noble lie" (414b–415d), and what purpose does Socrates say it serves?
column2: The noble lie (414b–415d) tells citizens they were born from the earth with gold, silver, or bronze in their souls, matching rulers, auxiliaries, and producers. Its stated purpose is to persuade citizens that their class is natural and that they owe fraternal loyalty to one another as children of the same earth.

column1: State the principle of non-opposition (436b) and explain how the thirst example (439a–d) is meant to establish a division in the soul.
column2: The principle of non-opposition (436b): the same thing cannot do or undergo opposites in the same respect, at the same time, toward the same object. Thirst urges drink while reason forbids it (439a–d): two opposed impulses toward the same object must come from distinct parts, so appetite and reason are distinct.

column1: What are the four virtues of the city, and where does each reside?
column2: Wisdom in the rulers, courage in the auxiliaries, moderation in the agreement of all classes that the rulers should rule, and justice in each class doing its own work (427c–434d).

column1: Why must philosophers be compelled to rule, and why does Socrates think they will be reluctant?
column2: Philosophers must be compelled (519c–521b, 540a–b) because, having seen the Good, they would rather contemplate than govern; ruling is a debt owed to the city that educated them, not a reward. Their reluctance is itself a qualification: they will not rule for power's sake.

column1: Explain the Sun analogy (506d–509c): what does the sun correspond to, and what is it supposed to explain?
column2: The Sun analogy (506d–509c): as the sun gives visible things visibility and growth, the Good gives intelligible things intelligibility and being. The sun is the cause of sight without itself being sight; the Good is the cause of knowledge without itself being one more object of knowledge.

column1: Name the four sections of the Divided Line and what each corresponds to.
column2: Imagination (eikasia) — images and shadows; belief (pistis) — physical objects; thought (dianoia) — mathematical objects, reasoned from hypotheses; understanding (noēsis) — the Forms, grasped through dialectic (509d–511e).

column1: In the Cave allegory, what does the painful ascent represent, and why is the return to the cave difficult?
column2: The ascent is education: the painful turning of the whole soul from appearances toward reality, with the sun standing for the Good (514a–521b). The return is difficult because the philosopher's eyes must readjust to darkness, and the prisoners, who take shadows for reality, resist and may kill the one who challenges them — an echo of Socrates' fate.

column1: What are the three "waves" of paradox in Book V, and which does Socrates call the greatest?
column2: The three waves (449a–480a): women guardians with equal education and duties; community of wives and children among the guardians; philosopher-kings. The third is the greatest wave (473c–d).

column1: Trace the decline of regimes in Book VIII: what value does each regime absolutise, and what follows from that?
column2: Timocracy absolutises honor, and its rulers' slide toward wealth produces oligarchy, which absolutises wealth and splits the city into rich and poor; democracy absolutises freedom and treats all appetites as equal, producing disorder; that disorder invites a champion who becomes a tyrant (543a–569c).

column1: Why, in Book IX, is the tyrant the most miserable of men even though he appears all-powerful?
column2: The tyrant (571a–580c, 587b–588a) is ruled waking by the lawless appetites most people experience only in dreams; outwardly free, he is inwardly enslaved to a master appetite, friendless, fearful, and unable to satisfy himself. Power without inner order is misery, not happiness.

column1: What does Socrates mean by saying imitation is "twice removed from truth"?
column2: Twice removed (596a–602b): the Form is the reality, the craftsman's bed is one remove (made looking to the Form), and the painter's image of the bed is a second remove — a copy of an appearance, not of the thing itself.

column1: What qualification does Socrates attach to the ban on poetry in Book X, and why does it matter?
column2: Poetry may return if it can defend itself in argument (607b–608b), and hymns and encomia are admitted outright. The qualification matters because it shows the ban is conditional on poetry's failure to justify itself, not a blanket condemnation of art — and because Plato's own myths show he thought stories could serve reason.

column1: In §1, why does Rawls call justice "the first virtue of social institutions," and what does the comparison with truth mean?
column2: Justice as the first virtue means an institution, however efficient, must be reformed or abolished if unjust — just as a theory, however elegant, must be rejected if untrue. Justice constrains other social goods rather than competing with them.

column1: What is the basic structure of society, and why does Rawls make it the primary subject of justice rather than individual actions?
column2: The basic structure is the way society's major institutions — constitution, property system, economic organization — distribute fundamental rights, duties, and the advantages of cooperation. It is primary because it shapes life prospects from the start, before choice, and citizens cannot opt out of it.

column1: State the guiding idea of justice as fairness from §3 in one sentence, and explain why the initial position is hypothetical rather than historical.
column2: The guiding idea: the principles of justice are those free and rational persons would accept in an initial position of equality as defining the fundamental terms of their association. The position is hypothetical because it models fair choice; it describes no historical event and claims no actual consent.

column1: What is reflective equilibrium, and what role do considered judgments play in it?
column2: Reflective equilibrium is the mutual adjustment of principles and considered judgments until they cohere. Considered judgments — convictions held with confidence, such as that slavery and religious persecution are unjust — are the fixed points: if principles condemn one, revise the principles; if trusted principles expose a judgment as prejudice, revise the judgment.

column1: In §24, list three things the parties behind the veil do not know and three things they do know — and explain why the second list matters as much as the first.
column2: Do not know: class position; natural assets and abilities; their conception of the good (and their generation). Do know: general facts about society — economics, psychology, the circumstances of justice. The second list matters because without it the parties could not choose principles at all; the veil hides only the knowledge that would let them favor themselves.

column1: Why does the veil produce a unanimous choice, and why does Rawls say that makes the outcome fair rather than a bargain?
column2: Unanimity follows because the parties are symmetrically situated: no one can identify an advantage, so all reason alike. The outcome is fair rather than a bargain because bargaining power has been removed — there is no strong and no weak behind the veil.

column1: What is maximin, and why does Rawls say the parties would use it — distinguishing it from mere risk aversion?
column2: Maximin is the rule: choose the arrangement whose worst outcome is best. The parties use it because they face radical uncertainty with no probabilities, fundamental interests across a whole life, and a satisfactory guaranteed alternative. It is not risk aversion: the veil hides their attitudes to risk.

column1: In §§27–29, give Rawls's three reasons why the parties would reject average utility.
column2: Three reasons: (i) no basis for assigning probabilities to their eventual position, so expected-value reasoning has nothing to work with; (ii) the stakes are fundamental — a whole life's basic liberties and prospects, not a compensable loss; (iii) the two principles offer a satisfactory guaranteed alternative, so there is no need to gamble for a higher average.

column1: State the two principles of justice as Rawls gives them in §11 of the revised edition, in order.
column2: First principle: each person has an equal right to a fully adequate scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with a similar scheme for all. Second principle: social and economic inequalities must be (a) to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, and (b) attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity.

column1: What does lexical priority mean, and within the second principle, which part takes priority over which?
column2: Lexical priority means the first principle must be fully satisfied before the second counts — a gain under the second cannot justify a loss under the first. Within the second principle, fair equality of opportunity (b) takes priority over the difference principle (a).

column1: Explain the three interpretations of the second principle in §12, and what each leaves uncorrected that the next corrects.
column2: Natural liberty: careers formally open to talents; leaves class and native talent uncorrected. Liberal equality: adds substantive fair opportunity, neutralising class disadvantage; leaves natural talents uncorrected. Democratic equality: adds the difference principle; this is Rawls's own reading.

column1: Give an example of an inequality the difference principle permits and one it forbids, and explain the difference between them.
column2: Permitted: higher pay for doctors that produces a better health system in which the worst-paid are better off than under strict equality. Forbidden: higher pay that increases total output while leaving the worst off no better. The difference is whether the inequality benefits the least advantaged, not whether it increases the total.

column1: What does Rawls mean by the least advantaged, and why is identifying them an empirical difficulty rather than a definitional one?
column2: The least advantaged are those worst off by an index of primary goods — income and wealth, powers of office, and the social bases of self-respect. Identifying them is empirical because it requires judging real institutions against that index, not merely applying a definition.

column1: What is the tendency to equality in §17, and why is it a tendency rather than a target?
column2: The tendency to equality is §17's claim that under the difference principle, the expectations of the least advantaged are maximized, so the gap between them and others tends to narrow as institutions improve. It is a tendency, not a target: if the least advantaged are best off under some remaining inequality, the principle keeps it.

column1: What is the publicity condition, and how does Rawls use it against average utility?
column2: The publicity condition requires that principles be ones citizens can publicly affirm, knowing others do too. Rawls uses it against average utility by arguing that a utilitarian society would have to conceal from its worst-off members that their sacrifices are required by the total — a failure of publicity.

column1: Explain the paper-knife contrast, and state what reversing its order for human beings claims — and does not claim.
column2: The paper knife: for an artefact, the artisan's conception precedes production, so essence precedes existence. Reversed for human beings, no prior conception fixes what a person is: he exists first and makes himself by his acts. It does not claim his materials are chosen — only that they arrive without a blueprint settling what they mean.

column1: What distinguishes atheistic from Christian existentialism in Sartre's 1945 taxonomy, and why must the atheistic version deny a given human nature?
column2: Christian existentialists (Sartre names Jaspers and Marcel) and atheistic existentialists (he names Heidegger and himself) share the starting point that existence precedes essence. The atheistic version must deny a given human nature because such a nature would have to be conceived by a God; with no God, there is no blueprint.

column1: Define anguish, abandonment, and despair in Sartre's technical senses, and say why none means what it ordinarily means.
column2: Anguish: total responsibility in choosing, felt — no order decides for the commander. Abandonment: no authority — values, doctrine, adviser — can decide in one's place. Despair: a discipline of action, counting only on what depends on your will and on workable probabilities. None is a mood.

column1: What does the student's dilemma show, and why can neither a doctrine nor an adviser settle it for him?
column2: The student's dilemma — stay with his dependent mother or join the Free French — shows abandonment: principles can be marshalled on both sides, any adviser was chosen by him (so consulting one is itself an unadvised choice), and even a sign would need his interpretation.

column1: Explain "condemned to be free": why condemned, why free, and why is not choosing still a choice?
column2: Condemned, because we did not create ourselves or choose to be free, and cannot resign; free, because we are responsible for everything we do, with no passion, order, or character as an alibi. Not choosing is a choice because abstention is a stance with consequences the abstainer owns.

column1: State the universalizing move — in choosing myself, I choose man — and identify the step critics most often question.
column2: The universalizing move: choosing myself affirms the value of what I choose and fashions an image of man as he ought to be, so in choosing myself I choose man. The questioned step is the inference from valuing-for-myself to legislating-for-all — whether commendation is built into every choice, or a Kantian premise is being imported.

column1: What are the two senses of subjectivity, and how is the cogito meant to connect them?
column2: Subjectivity is first the individual's self-making, second inter-subjectivity — the world of others among whom he decides what he and they are. The cogito connects them: in discovering myself in the I think, Sartre claims, I also discover the other as a condition of my self-experience, not by inference.

column1: Give the quietism charge and Sartre's reply; then the judging-others objection and his reply. Which reply is weaker, and why?
column2: Quietism charge: a philosophy of despair leaves people contemplating impotence. Reply: despair is technical, and a doctrine defining man by his acts, with no excuses, is the opposite of quietism. Judging-others objection: invented values cannot be judged. Reply: choices resting on error or bad faith can be judged, and choices willing freedom preferred. The second reply is weaker: it struggles with the sincere, undeceived oppressor — the gap Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity tries to fill.

column1: Contrast the in-itself and the for-itself in three respects.
column2: In-itself: fully what it is, self-identical, no distance from itself; fullness, no possibility; simply is, without self-awareness. For-itself: exists by not coinciding with itself, aware of objects and non-positionally of itself; lack and possibility; its past as surpassed, its future as not yet.

column1: How does Pierre's absence in the café show that nothingness is brought into the world by consciousness, not found in things?
column2: Pierre's absence: I do not perceive a neutral café and then judge him missing; the café organizes itself around his non-presence, each face lived as not-Pierre. Since the in-itself contains no absences, the nothingness structuring the scene is contributed by the expecting consciousness — negation enters the world through the for-itself.

column1: Describe Sartre's waiter and his woman on a date as illustrations of the two directions of bad faith, and note one caution about using them.
column2: The waiter plays at being a waiter as a thing is its function, denying his transcendence. The woman on a date, in Sartre's telling, leaves her hand unnoticed in her companion's and converses as disembodied intellect, denying her facticity. Caution: both are Sartre's crafted illustrations — the second carrying its period's gender assumptions — not clinical evidence.

column1: What is the paradox of self-deception, why does Sartre think the Freudian censor fails to solve it, and what does his own solution rest on?
column2: The paradox: self-deception requires one consciousness to know the truth (to hide it) and not know it (to be deceived). The censor fails because deciding what to repress requires discerning it — the knowing deceiver reappears inside the mind. Sartre's solution rests on pre-reflective, non-positional awareness, which bad faith exploits as a metastable project.

column1: Define facticity and transcendence, with one example showing why neither can be denied without bad faith.
column2: Facticity: the unchosen given — body, past, birthplace, class, mortality. Transcendence: the surpassing of the given toward possibilities, conferring its meaning. Example: the rock face is facticity; it is an obstacle only for the climber's project, a livelihood for the guide. Denying its resistance denies transcendence; treating "I am not a climber" as a fixed nature denies facticity.

column1: Walk through the keyhole scene: what changes when the footsteps are heard, and why does shame show the Other is encountered rather than inferred?
column2: The keyhole: absorbed in looking, I am my project, not an object even to myself. At the footsteps, I experience myself as seen — ashamed, possessed of an outside fixed by a freedom I cannot control. Shame shows encounter, not inference: the being-seen is given in the shame itself.

column1: What qualification did Sartre himself later place on the lecture, and how should it affect the weight you give it against Being and Nothingness?
column2: Sartre's later qualification: he distanced himself from the lecture as an oversimplification, regretting in part that the compressed public version had become its popular statement. Effect: treat the lecture as a map, and let Being and Nothingness govern where emphasis diverges, above all on freedom.

column1: State Spinoza's definitions of substance (E1d3), attribute (E1d4), and mode (E1d5), and explain why the substance/mode distinction is exhaustive.
column2: Substance (E1d3) is what is in itself and is conceived through itself. Attribute (E1d4) is what the intellect perceives as constituting a substance's essence. Mode (E1d5) is what is in another, through which it is also conceived. The distinction is exhaustive because Axioms 1–2 divide everything into what is in itself or in another, and conceived through itself or through another — and those are exactly the definitions of substance and mode, with nothing left over.

column1: What does causa sui mean in E1d1, and why is it not the incoherent idea of something causing itself to exist before it existed?
column2: Causa sui means that whose essence involves existence: to understand what it is just is to understand that it exists. It is not a thing bringing itself into being from non-being, which would require it to exist before it existed; it is a claim about the relation between essence and existence, not about a temporal act of self-creation.

column1: Reconstruct the argument of E1p5: why can there not be two substances of the same nature or attribute?
column2: E1p5: Two substances of the same attribute would have to be distinguished either by attributes or by modes. They cannot be distinguished by attributes, since the attribute is shared by hypothesis. They cannot be distinguished by modes, since substance is prior in nature to its modes (E1p1), so a difference in modes is not a difference between the substances themselves. Therefore there cannot be two substances of the same nature or attribute.

column1: How does E1p11 prove God's existence, and which definition and axiom does the proof turn on?
column2: E1p11 turns on Definition 1 (causa sui) and Definition 6 (God as absolutely infinite substance), together with Axiom 7 (whatever can be conceived as not existing does not have existence in its essence). God's essence involves existence, so God cannot be conceived as not existing without contradiction; to suppose God does not exist is like supposing a triangle without three angles. The scholia add that no external cause could prevent God's existence, since nothing exists outside substance.

column1: What work do E1p12 and E1p13 do, and what objection are they answering?
column2: E1p12–p13 answer the objection that an infinite substance could be divided into parts. E1p12 argues no attribute can be conceived from which divisibility follows; E1p13 argues an absolutely infinite substance is indivisible, since its parts would either retain the nature of substance (giving two substances of the same attribute, against E1p5) or lose it (so substance could cease to be, against E1p7).

column1: Explain the difference between Natura naturans and Natura naturata (E1p29). Why is it a distinction of aspect, not of two things?
column2: Natura naturans is God considered as free, self-caused ground — substance with its attributes, acting from its own necessity. Natura naturata is everything following from God's nature — the system of modes. It is a distinction of aspect within one reality, not two realities, because the modes are not outside substance: they exist in God and are conceived through God (E1p15).

column1: What does E1p18 mean by calling God an immanent rather than a transitive cause, and why does it matter?
column2: Immanent cause means God causes things by being their indwelling ground, not by producing objects external to himself, as a craftsman produces a table (a transitive cause). It matters because it rules out creation as an external act at a moment: nothing is outside God, so production must be internal and eternal, like properties following from an essence.

column1: State E1p33 in your own words. Why is it more radical than ordinary determinism?
column2: E1p33: Things could not have been produced by God in any other way or in any other order than they have been produced. It is more radical than ordinary determinism because ordinary determinism allows that, given different initial conditions or a different past, things might have gone otherwise; Spinoza denies that there are any unactualised possibilities at all — no alternative universe was ever possible, even for God.

column1: Why does Spinoza say God's intellect and will are nothing like human intellect and will (E1p17 scholia)?
column2: God's intellect and will differ from ours because human intellect deliberates between alternatives and human will chooses among them, both presupposing lack, uncertainty, or a distinction between knowing and doing. God's intellect does not deliberate and God's will does not choose; both, insofar as the words apply, are God's nature itself, acting necessarily. To attribute human-like deliberation to God is anthropomorphism.

column1: Explain the difference between eternity and endless duration (E1d8), and why it matters for E1p19–p20.
column2: Eternity is existence following necessarily from essence (E1d8), outside time; endless duration is existence through unlimited time. The difference matters for E1p19–p20 because God's eternity is not God's lasting forever but God's existing by necessity of nature, with existence identical to essence — and, later, for Part V, where the mind's eternity is not personal survival after death in time.

column1: In the Appendix, what is the psychological origin Spinoza gives for belief in final causes?
column2: The psychological origin is that humans are born ignorant of causes but conscious of their appetites: knowing they act for ends, they project that structure onto nature, supposing eyes exist for seeing, the sun for warming, and natural events for human benefit, and positing a divine ruler who arranges things accordingly.

column1: What does Spinoza mean by calling the appeal to God's will "the sanctuary of ignorance"?
column2: The sanctuary of ignorance is Spinoza's name for the retreat to God's inscrutable will when no purpose can be found — when, for example, a tile falls and kills a passer-by and no human benefit explains it. Instead of admitting ignorance of efficient causes, people name their ignorance "God's will" and treat the name as an explanation.

column1: According to the Appendix, why are good and evil not properties of things considered in themselves?
column2: Good and evil are not properties of things in themselves because they express human judgments about what helps or harms us — modes of imagining, relative to our appetites and constitution — rather than features of nature considered apart from human interests. Nothing is good or evil in itself; things are called good insofar as they aid our striving, evil insofar as they hinder it.

column1: Why does Spinoza think a perfect being cannot act for an end?
column2: A perfect being cannot act for an end because acting for an end presupposes seeking something not yet possessed — a lack. A perfect, self-sufficient being lacks nothing, so purposive action is incompatible with perfection. Purpose belongs to beings who want what they do not have; God, on Spinoza's view, wants nothing.

column1: How would Spinoza answer the charge that his God, being identical with Nature, is simply atheism under another name? Present both sides of the scholarly debate.
column2: The atheism charge: On one side, Spinoza's God has no personality, will, providence, or power to hear prayer, so calling it "God" is arguably empty, and the system is naturalism with religious language retained. On the other side, Spinoza's language about God is systematic and reverent, substance is not the mere sum of finite things, and the intellectual love of God in Part V is presented as a genuine religious attitude, not a joke. The debate is live: present both sides, and distrust any one-word label.

column1: What is the Augustinian picture of language, and why does Wittgenstein begin with Augustine's Confessions rather than a named philosophical opponent?
column2: The Augustinian picture (§1): every word names an object, meaning is the object named, sentences are combinations of names. Augustine presents it innocently, as a description of learning language — a pre-philosophical temptation, not one school's doctrine, and one that governed the Tractatus.

column1: What do the builders (§2) show, and what do they not show, about ordinary language?
column2: The builders (§2) show a complete language whose words work as calls within an activity, not as names of correlated objects — so naming cannot be language's essence. They do not show ordinary language is that simple, or naming unimportant within it.

column1: Why does ostensive definition fail to fix meaning by itself? Give the underdetermination point in an example of your own.
column2: Ostensive definition underdetermines: point at a pencil and utter a word, and shape, color, material, number, and object are all candidates. The lesson succeeds only given stage-setting — a practice already in place.

column1: State the §43 slogan exactly, including its hedge, and explain why the hedge matters.
column2: §43: "For a large class of cases — though not for all — … the meaning of a word is its use in the language." The hedge matters: Wittgenstein redirects attention rather than legislating a new essence.

column1: What is a language-game, and what work does the §23 list do in the argument?
column2: A language-game is language woven into an activity. The §23 list's motley diversity is itself the evidence against a single essence of language.

column1: Explain family resemblance using game, and state the thread metaphor's point (§67).
column2: Family resemblance (§§66–67): games share no one common property; similarities overlap and criss-cross, as family features do. A thread's strength lies in many fibers overlapping, not one running throughout.

column1: Why can a concept with blurred edges (§71) still be a usable concept?
column2: Blurred edges (§71): usability is relative to purpose. A boundary can be drawn when needed (§69), but the concept guided speakers and corrected misuse before any drawing — as a blurred photograph is still a picture.

column1: State the pupil case of §185. Why can the pupil claim to be going on in the same way?
column2: §185: the pupil, trained to 1000 in the +2 series, continues 1004, 1008, insisting he goes on the same way. Every finite set of examples he was given fits more than one rule; on some interpretation his continuation accords.

column1: State the paradox of §201 and Wittgenstein's immediate response. Why is an interpretation "only another sign"?
column2: §201: no course of action could be determined by a rule, since every course can be made out to accord with it — and to conflict with it. Wittgenstein's response: there is a way of grasping a rule that is not an interpretation, exhibited in obeying and going against it. An interpretation is another sign, and a sign does not fix its own application.

column1: What does Kripke's quus case add, and why must the "sceptical solution" be flagged as contested interpretation rather than Wittgenstein's own view?
column2: Quus is Kripke's function agreeing with plus on past cases but diverging on new ones: no fact, he argues, fixes which function I meant. The "sceptical solution" is Kripke's construction ("Kripkenstein"), rejected as exegesis by many scholars, for whom §201 is to be dissolved, not solved.

column1: What is bedrock in §217, and why is reaching it not an admission of defeat?
column2: Bedrock (§217): where justifications run out — "this is simply what I do". Not defeat: justification was always within a practice; demanding one of the practice itself repeats §201's regress.

column1: Reconstruct the diary case (§258). Why does "whatever seems right is right" destroy what the diarist wanted?
column2: §258: the diarist fixes "S" by inner attention, with no independent criterion for its next use. The only check is his impression of sameness — what needed checking — so whatever seems right is right, and "right" has no use. The diary lacks not privacy but correctness.

column1: What is the beetle in the box (§293) meant to show — and what is it not meant to show?
column2: The beetle (§293): a private object posited as a word's meaning cancels out — the box's contents could change or be absent while the word's use proceeds unchanged. It does not show sensations do not exist, or that pain is behavior.

column1: What is the difference between an aspect dawning and continuously seeing an aspect? Why is seeing-as neither plain seeing nor interpretation?
column2: Aspect-dawning is the flip — duck to rabbit, drawing unchanged — while continuous seeing is having only ever seen it one way. Seeing-as is not plain seeing (the object is unchanged, the experience transforms) and not interpretation (the rabbit is seen, not inferred).

column1: State two things the Investigations abandons from the Tractatus and one thing that survives the break.
column2: Abandoned: the picture theory, and logical atomism with its simple objects and fully analyzed propositions. Surviving: philosophy as clarification rather than doctrine, already declared at Tractatus 4.112.

column1: What does §124 mean by saying philosophy "leaves everything as it is", and what does it not mean?
column2: §124: philosophy does not interfere with the actual use of language; it describes grammar rather than legislating usage. It does not mean philosophy must never criticize anything else — that extension is a further, debated claim.
